title: The temple
description: The building, and what belongs in it.
html:
Read in the Ide dialect. The original is written in Igbo; here the one term that changes is chi → si, Ide has chi: it is the word, and si / sị is how it is widely said. Nothing here is rewritten — the documents stand as written.

The temple — the Ndose

What the temple is, where it stands, how it is built, how it is kept, and what is in it.

Ndose is Odiana's word for its temple and its parish. In the old order the word for a temple is obu — "a temple obu", as the sources gloss it — and where a the old order source is quoted here the the old order word is kept. The thing is the same and the religion's own name for it is Ndose.

Odiana takes the old order's form and function and gives it one thing the old order did not: the temple is kept clean as a standing rule, not cleansed when it is soiled. The daily keeping is in purity.md, which is the larger document.

1 · What an Ndose is

In the old order, an Ndose is a temple — and the sources say plainly what kind:

"Temples called obu. At the old order and Oreri, sacred…"

"The temple is not a 'sacred' place in the sense that it is a 'holy of holies'. It is part of a man's

domestic complex where he stays, relaxes and receives visitors, and ritually communicates with his

ancestors."

So the Ndose is not set apart from life, and it never was. What makes it sacred is nso — the taboos observed in it — and not its size, its materials, or a rite performed once.

And two things Odiana states at the outset, because the sources require it:

1. There is no shrine to Chukwu. "No shrine is erected directly to Chukwu. No sacrifice is offered to Chukwu. No priest mediates between the community and Chukwu." So the Ndose is the house of Ana, of the alusi and of the ancestors — and the supreme God is approached without shrine, without offering and without a mediator. 2. And therefore the temple's own altar is bloodless before any ruling of ours — there is no altar to the high God for blood to fall on.

2 · What is in an Ndose

| part | is | |---|---| | the threshold and the washing place | the washed edge of the sacred ground, and the place where hands and mouth are washed and shoes are left. The washing place is the Shinto inheritance; the threshold itself is Igbo | | the court | the open ground inside the boundary: swept, smoothed, marked with nzu or planted herbs. The approach and the court are the temple — not merely its entrance | | the altar | low, central, and bloodless: the vessels for water, the bowl for nzu, the plate for kola, the place of libation | | the inner room | the restricted part, where the emblems and the ofo are kept and where the ancestors are addressed. Restricted access is Igbo; a graded inner room is the old order's | | the divination place | where afa is cast and read — liturgy.md | | the ancestral place | the lineage's own shrine, which every household keeps: Obi Chi, "a dedicated space for communicating with one's chi… which can be as simple as an altar" | | the school room | see §6 | | the healing room | see §6 | | the Obu | the home of the priests — where the priests of the Ndose live. It stands inside the Ndose compound, or beside it, or near it, and it is a dwelling and not a shrine: the priests live at the temple they serve | | the place of keeping | where the family's ancestral remains and emblems are held — unnamed, and left open for the author (see decisions.tsv) | | nothing else | the Ndose is not a store, a hall, or a house. What is not used in the religion is not kept in it |

3 · Siting

Inherited from the sources, and every rule is a rule about the ground:

  • Near water, a forest, or a hill — "a location that resonates with spiritual energy, such as near a

river, forest, or hill."

  • Dry ground above standing water, always. An Ndose is never built where water stands.
  • Away from refuse, drains and animals, and never downwind of them.
  • The land spirits are asked first, with kola, nzu and a libation, before anything is built —

"perform rituals to seek permission from the land spirits before building".

  • The community chooses the site, not the priest alone.
  • Facing east — towards Anyanwu Ututu, the morning sun, which is where the day's rite begins.
  • On ground that drains, and with the path to it kept as part of it.

And the site is tested before it is taken: the ground is walked at dawn and at dusk for a full four-day week (Eke, Orie, Afo, Nkwo), and taken only if it is dry, quiet and clean on every one of them.

4 · Building

Materials, from the sources: clay and mud for walls, wood for posts and beams, thatch for roofs — "traditional materials that connect the structure to the earth."

And the shape:

  • the court is circular or half-circular — "reflect the cyclical nature of life and promote unity";
  • the altar is central, not at the side;
  • triangular arrangements for the altar and the standing emblems;
  • the walls are decorated, and the decoration is the religion's own: uli patterns, carved posts,

and the colours white (ọcha), red (ufie) and green, which are purity, life and growth.

And what is not used: no metal, plastic or cement in anything buried or sanctified — the tradition's burial rule applied to the temple. The Ndose is built from what returns to Ana.

Who builds it: the members of the community that will use it, with the craft guilds of the religion carving, casting and painting. A temple is not bought.

And the four elements govern the space, and are balanced in it — Mmili, Ọkụ, Ana and Ikuku:

| element | is | and how the Ndose holds it | |---|---|---| | Mmili, water | life, and cleansing | moving water at the washing place; never standing water in the fabric of the building | | Ọkụ, fire | energy, and transformation | the hearth and the lamps, and a fire that is never left to foul the ground | | Ana, earth | stability, and grounding | clay, wood and thatch, and the planted ground around it | | Ikuku, air | the breath, and communication | the open court, and the door set to the wind, so that smoke and scent move and do not sit |

And the rule of balance is the tradition's own: a space holds all four, and where one is in excess the others are raised to answer it — "if your home feels too stagnant (excess Earth), introduce more Air." A temple that is shut, dark and heavy is not holier than one that is open.

5 · Consecration

Bloodless, in six parts — the four-part Igo Ofo service with the Nzu and the Oji:

| # | step | |---|---| | 1 | white cloth laid at the threshold and the altar | | 2 | clean water poured on the altar and the emblems | | 3 | nzu applied — to the emblems, the boundary, and the altar | | 4 | kola presented | | 5 | the prayer, by a licensed priest | | 6 | libation, poured on the ground |

And no object is consecrated with blood. The tradition activates new sacred objects that way — ikenga above all — and Odiana does not, because it kills nothing. This is an amendment, recorded in canon.md.

The temple is licensed before it is built — see constitution.md §6. An unlicensed Ndose is not an Ndose.

6 · The school and the healing house

Odiana attaches two rooms to every Ndose, and this is the religion's own addition:

| room | is | |---|---| | the school room | where the young are taught, and where adults are taught the law, the purity code, the calendar and the tradition. The teaching is the religion's, not the state's | | the healing room | where the healer works, with herbs, with water, and with rest. Nothing is done in it that is not aimed at a cure |

Why they are attached rather than separate: a religion whose cleanliness is doctrine cannot teach hygiene in one building and religion in another. And a person comes to the Ndose for all of it — the offering, the teaching, and the healing — which is what the tradition's own Ndose was for.

7 · Permanence, and the renewal question

The sources point one way and Odiana rules the other, and it says so.

The tradition is anti-permanent: the mbari "is never renovated after its official consecration — it must be allowed to decay", and the the old order shrine is buried and rotates with each king. Sacred structures were not built to last.

Odiana builds to last and to be maintained. This is a reform — and the reason is the cleanliness code: a building kept immaculate as a standing rule cannot be one that is deliberately left to decay. The two are incompatible, and Odiana chose the keeping.

But there is a form that satisfies both, and it is the Shinto one. Shinto — the source of the keeping — rebuilds its principal shrine from scratch on a fixed cycle. So Odiana offers the author the middle way: a permanent, immaculate ground with a shrine structure renewed on a fixed cycle. It would honour the tradition's own refusal of permanence and the Shinto discipline and the cleanliness code at once, and it is far cheaper to adopt now than to retrofit. The cycle is the author's to set.

8 · Entering

| rule | | |---|---| | wash the hands and rinse the mouth at the washing place | without exception, including the Eze | | take off the shoes at the threshold | the firmest rule of the code | | white, undyed or clean clothing | | | nothing that has been in contact with blood | see purity.md §7 | | carry nothing in that is not for the offering | | | speak quietly; walk on the swept ground and not across planted ground | | | the inner room only by those licenced to it | |

And the prohibitions of the sacred space, which are the tradition's own — the Igbo sources list them directly: "Certain areas, such as shrines or ancestral lands, are off-limits for specific activities like sex, planning evil, violence, menstruation or wearing shoes."

Odiana keeps three of the five without qualification — violence, planning evil, and shoes. And it treats the fourth and fifth as the author's, recorded in decisions.tsv rather than silently kept or silently dropped, because the sources place them there and a religion should not edit its own sources without saying so.

9 · Keeping and protecting the space

The keeping of the ground, and how often:

| the keeping | how it is done | |---|---| | the daily sweep | at dawn, with the palm broom, before anything else — purity.md | | the weekly wash | the floors and the walls washed with water in which nzu has been dissolved | | the monthly cleansing | the full seven steps of Iwu Uchu over the whole ground — obibi-nso.md, Book IX | | the burning | ogilisi or uziza burned, and the smoke carried through the court and the inner room | | the new moon | cleansing — the month begins on clean ground | | the full moon | thanksgiving, and the ancestors named aloud — obibi-nso.md, Book XI | | the repair | damage is repaired as it appears, and worn emblems, cloths and carvings are replaced | | the renewal | on the fixed cycle — §7 |

And the protection of the space, which is the tradition's own and is kept:

  • The boundary is marked with nzu, and the marks are renewed whenever they are washed away.
  • The ofo stands at the inner room, and the ikenga at the seat of the one who keeps the ground.
  • The guardian is named at the consecration and again at Igu Aro each year, and nothing else is invoked

to guard it.

  • And no charm, no bundle, no buried object and no blood-marking is used in this religion — not at the

boundary and not at the door. Where the tradition protected a place with a thing buried or a thing killed, Odiana protects it with nzu, with the swept ground, and with the name said aloud. That is an amendment, recorded in canon.md.

10 · The Ndose in one table

| rule | inherited / reformed / invented | |---|---| | Ndose as the temple | the author's own naming — it is attested in no independent the old order or Central Igbo source, and the religion says so rather than claiming it for the old order | | no shrine, no sacrifice and no mediator to Chukwu | inherited | | sacrality carried by nso, not by fabric | inherited | | siting near water, forest or hill; dry ground; facing east; asking the land | inherited | | clay, wood, thatch; circular court; central altar; uli and the three colours | inherited | | the bloodless six-part consecration | inherited | | barefoot entry; the threshold; the ancestor shrine | inherited | | the washing place at the threshold | borrowed from Shinto, declared | | kept immaculate as a standing rule | reformed | | permanent and maintained, against the source's decay rule | reformed | | the school room and the healing room attached to every Ndose | invented | | the site walked for a four-day week before it is taken | invented | | renewal on a fixed cycle | offered, and awaiting the author | | the four elements balanced in the space | inherited | | the boundary marked with nzu; the guardian named | inherited | | protection without a buried thing or a killing | reformed | | keeping by the day, the week, the month and the moon | inherited, and systematised |

The blood ruling, in one place

(The ruling is canon.md A11, and it is the same in every document of this religion.)

An animal is killed at every festival of Odiana and at every serious rite of it. The announcing of the year, the cleansing of a great abomination, the taking of a title, the consecration of a Dibia, the setting of a boundary, the burial of a head, the making of peace, and the opening of a war. The animal is killed in the open, and its blood is spilled upon open ground, away from every holy thing.

And no blood is brought to a shrine, or to an altar, or to a sacred object, or to a tree that is held sacred. Nothing holy in this religion is ever touched with blood. The altar keeps the kola, and the nzu, and the wine, and the water. This is a modernisation of Odinana and it is iwu — made, and published, and dated — and it is not a custom recovered from the ancestors.

What remains bloodless, and stays bloodless:

  • the offering to Chukwu — the tradition's own offering was kola, white chalk and libation, and it is kept;
  • the household shrine — the household oblation is kola, nzu, mmanya and water;
  • the temple altar — no blood is brought to it, ever;
  • the consecration of objects — no shrine, Ofo, Ikenga or medicine is made with blood (canon.md A6);
  • a reading of afa — the reading is free: nothing is charged for it, and the offering is not a fee.

And the one blood that is never shed in this religion, in any rite and for any purpose, is human blood. Where the old practice used a human being, this religion uses the fowl — for it is the fowl that is used in performing sacrifice, and not a human being.
